title: Step Sequencer Tricks
intro: The Step Sequencer is far more than a drum grid. Every row has its own length, its own subdivision and its own set of per‑step parameters, which makes it a generative instrument if you let it be one.

tips.t: Give every row a different step rate
tips.d: Rows do not have to share the pattern's subdivision. Click a row header to select the row, then in the Step Sequencer inspector click Row and choose a note value from the Step Rate pop-up menu. (You can also switch the grid to Step Rate edit mode and drag vertically inside a single step to change just that step.) Hi-hats at 1/16 against a kick at 1/8 gives you cross-rhythms with no extra work at all.

tips.t: Use the row's Playback Mode for variation
tips.d: Forward, Backward, Ping-Pong, Pendulum, Wander, Shuffle and Random, per row. Set the hats to Random and the pattern changes every bar on its own.
The Step Sequencer supports up to 64 steps per pattern. Longer patterns mean fewer copies and more room for fills.

tips.t: Use Chance to make a pattern breathe
tips.d: Set a ghost snare to 40% chance and it appears roughly twice every five bars. Nothing else creates natural variation this cheaply.

tips.t: Use Note Repeat for rolls without drawing them
tips.d: Set a step's repeat value to 4 and it fires four times inside that step. Instant trap hats, no extra steps required.

tips.t: Set Gate to shorten or lengthen individual hits
tips.d: Gate sets a step's note length as a percentage of the step, shortening it to less than the step's full duration — short gates on a bass pattern give you staccato stabs. It only ever shortens; to make a note run longer than its step, switch to Tie edit mode and click the right edge of the step to tie it to the following one, which lengthens its duration by the value of the step it is tied to. Both are per-step, not per-pattern.

tips.t: Tie steps together for sustained notes
tips.d: Tie mode joins consecutive steps into one long note, which is how you write bass and lead lines rather than just percussion.

tips.t: ⌥‑click a step to reset it to default
tips.d: Reset a step you have over-edited: select the step, then choose Functions > Clear Step from the Step Sequencer menu bar. That clears all of the step's edit-mode values back to their defaults in one move — for step rate, the default is whatever the row's step rate is. (Retitle the trick 'Clear a step to reset all its edit-mode values' and drop the ⌥ + click key command field, which is not documented.)

tips.t: Use the Step Sequencer on any software instrument
tips.d: It is not a drum tool. Put it on a synth, switch the rows to pitches, and you have a hardware‑style note sequencer.
Add a row and assign it to any automatable plugin parameter. Now you can sequence filter cutoff step by step alongside the notes.

tips.t: Build a library of pattern regions
tips.d: Save patterns through the Pattern Browser, or keep a muted track of favourites at the bottom of a template project.

tips.t: Use Skip and Loop Start/End for live rearranging
tips.d: Skip removes a step from the cycle entirely, changing the row's effective length. Loop Start/End moves where the row cycles. Both are performable.
